challenges.judge_assessment: The attack correctly identifies a statutory-logic gap. The words “may be had” identify circumstances in which an FED proceeding is available; they do not themselves create a substantive privilege to use self-help. Source 72 also confirms that Chapter 1923 reaches defined defendants beyond conventional tenants. But that source does not establish that FED is exclusive for every occupier, so it does not itself prove Lee’s ultimate position. The brief has a substantial response in R.C. 5321.15(A), Ogle, and Stone, which it reads as making exclusivity depend on residential tenancy. Still, the brief’s reliance on the isolated word “may” contributes little. If the cited wrongful-eviction cases do not govern this employment-linked occupancy, the brief lacks a clear affirmative source authorizing summary removal.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant is correct that the phrase "proceedings under this chapter may be had" does not itself create a free-standing right of self-help. The point is narrower: Chapter 1923 identifies the circumstances in which an FED action may be brought, and R.C. 5321.15(A) makes FED the exclusive remedy only in the residential landlord-tenant setting. Because the record does not establish that Appellant was a tenant under a rental agreement, Appellant cannot convert the availability of FED into a requirement that Defendants proceed only by FED before ending an employment-based occupancy.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on the word "may" as if it authorizes self-help. Recast the point to show that Chapter 1923 identifies when FED proceedings are available, while R.C. 5321.15(A) makes FED exclusive only for residential tenants, and this case falls outside that class on the record.

challenges.opponent_argument: The categorical assertion that employee housing receives statutory protection only when there is a “separate” rental agreement and cash rent adds requirements not contained in the cited definition. challenges.why_it_matters: If the employment agreement itself can govern residential occupancy, the brief cannot exclude live-in caregivers, nannies, clergy, and every other listed employee category as a matter of law merely because there was no separate lease or cash-rent payment.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief’s categorical statement that protection exists only when an employee has a separate rental agreement and pays cash rent is broader than the cited statutory definition. R.C. 5321.01 does not expressly require that the occupancy agreement be separate from an employment contract, and the employee-tenant material indicates that employment and tenancy can coexist. Thus the brief cannot defend its sweeping list of caregivers, nannies, clergy, and other workers on statutory text alone. The defect does not automatically make Lee a tenant: the record may still establish that her room was a revocable workplace accommodation rather than premises she was entitled to occupy to the exclusion of others. The advocate risks losing the categorical legal rule and having the case judged under the actual terms of Lee’s arrangement.
challenges.suggested_response: The issue is not whether a rental agreement must always be a separate document or whether an employee can never be a tenant. The issue is whether this record shows that Appellant was entitled under any oral or written agreement to use and occupy the premises to the exclusion of others. It does not. The evidence shows only that she was given a room to stay in while working and that she remained an at-will employee who kept a separate residence. On this record, there is no basis to treat the employment accommodation as a residential tenancy.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Delete the sweeping statement that employee housing is protected only when there is a separate lease and cash rent. Replace it with the narrower proposition that, whatever form an agreement takes, the record here does not show a rental agreement or an exclusive possessory right.

challenges.opponent_argument: Ogle, Stone, and Amick do not establish that cash rent is indispensable in every employment-linked occupancy. As presented in the supplied material, Ogle and Stone involved persons living with others without a rental agreement, while Amick expressly emphasized that the occupant furnished no consideration. The present theory concerns housing furnished in connection with employment, a recognized employee-tenant setting. Thus, the material question is whether services or employment obligations constituted consideration for agreed occupancy—not simply whether Appellant wrote a rent check. [8]
challenges.why_it_matters: The cited cases cease to be dispositive if Appellant’s services supplied consideration and the employment arrangement established occupancy terms; at minimum, their different consideration facts prevent a categorical extension at summary judgment.

challenges.judge_assessment: The distinctions are legitimate. As the brief describes them, Ogle and Stone involved gratuitous domestic occupancy, and Amick expressly found both no agreement and no consideration. Lee, by contrast, was required to remain overnight to perform paid services. Those differences prevent treating the cases as mechanically dispositive without examining the employment bargain. The attack overreaches to the extent it assumes that services were consideration for the room: services may have been exchanged solely for wages, with overnight access remaining a revocable license. The brief has evidence supporting that characterization, but it does not squarely analyze whether the employment agreement allocated part of Lee’s compensation to an exclusive possessory right.
challenges.suggested_response: Ogle, Stone, and Amick remain instructive because each turned on the absence of a rental agreement and the absence of consideration for a tenancy. Appellant’s situation is different only if the employment arrangement itself granted an enforceable right to exclusive residential occupancy as part of the bargain. The record here does not show that. It shows a room provided as an accommodation while Appellant was on duty, an at-will employment relationship, and a separate residence maintained by Appellant. Those facts do not transform a work-related accommodation into a rental tenancy merely because Appellant slept on the premises.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the case distinctions, but make the point expressly about consideration and exclusive occupancy. Say the cited cases involved gratuitous occupancy, whereas the record here shows only permission to stay while working, not proof that housing was bargained for as rent.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack lands, although its assertion that the relevant facts are absent is inaccurate. The brief itself states that John Wallace and Sally Wallace jointly decided to terminate Lee. That evidence conflicts with the later assertion that the Estate had “no involvement.” John’s physical absence during the removal and Lee’s testimony that he did not personally order her out do not negate prior authorization or participation in the joint decision. challenges.suggested_response: Whether John Wallace was physically present at the moment Appellant left the premises is not the dispositive issue. The dispositive issue is that Appellant was not a tenant under a rental agreement and therefore cannot maintain a wrongful-eviction claim on the record before the Court. To the extent Appellant relies on John Wallace’s absence from the premises at the time of departure, that does not alter the summary-judgment analysis.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Drop the claim that the Estate had "no involvement" in the removal. challenges.opponent_argument: Northfield Park does not support the broad proposition asserted here. As quoted in the supplied material, that decision concerned a commercial lease containing a voluntarily accepted self-help provision and repossession occurring without breach of the peace and with the lessee’s acquiescence. This case concerns residential occupancy, and the brief identifies no comparable contractual self-help provision or acquiescence. The decision’s commercial-premises reasoning therefore cannot establish a general self-help right against residential occupants.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without extending a narrowly described commercial-lease holding beyond its facts, the brief lacks authority for its central claim that a residential homeowner may summarily remove every non-tenant occupant.

target.excerpt: The Ohio legislature has not mandated FED procedures to be required in all situations where a "tenant holds over his term" or "the defendant is an occupier of land or tenements". As acknowledged previously by this court in Northfield Park Associates v. Northeast Ohio Harness (1987), 36 Ohio App.3d 1

challenges.judge_assessment: Northfield Park cannot carry the residential self-help proposition asserted here. As the brief’s own quotation shows, that case involved a commercial lease containing an agreed self-help provision, peaceful repossession, and the lessee’s acquiescence. Those limitations are absent here. The decision is useful only by analogy for the narrower proposition that Chapter 1923 is not universally exclusive. The brief does not lose its entire position because Ogle and Stone address residential lockouts more directly, but it loses Northfield Park as affirmative authority for a general right to remove non-tenant residential occupants summarily.
challenges.suggested_response: Northfield Park does not supply a general residential self-help rule. As the quoted passage shows, it concerned a commercial lease with an agreed self-help provision and repossession without a breach of the peace and with the lessee’s acquiescence. That is not this case. Here, the relevant point is that R.C. 5321.15(A) makes FED exclusive in the residential landlord-tenant context, and the record does not establish that Appellant was a tenant under any rental agreement. Northfield Park therefore may be cited only for the limited proposition that Chapter 1923 is not universally exclusive in every setting.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Use Northfield Park only as a limited analogy, not as authority for a general self-help rule. Make clear it involved a commercial lease and an express self-help clause, and that the present case stands or falls on the absence of a tenant relationship under R.C. 5321.15(A).

attacks_proposed.argument: The absence of a separate lease document or cash-rent payment does not by itself establish the absence of a tenancy. R.C. 5321.01 defines a tenant through entitlement under a rental agreement, and a rental agreement may be any written or oral agreement establishing terms concerning use and occupancy. The governing definitions therefore require examination of the parties’ agreement and the consideration exchanged, not merely whether an instrument labeled “lease” existed or money was deducted as rent. Ohio landlord-tenant authority also recognizes that an employee may reside in residential premises pursuant to an employment contract as an employee tenant. [2, 6, 8]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the employment arrangement supplied the terms and consideration for Appellant’s required occupancy, tenancy cannot be rejected categorically on the two grounds relied upon by the trial court, and summary judgment on that basis cannot stand.

attacks_proposed.argument: Ogle, Stone, and Amick do not establish that cash rent is indispensable in every employment-linked occupancy. As presented in the supplied material, Ogle and Stone involved persons living with others without a rental agreement, while Amick expressly emphasized that the occupant furnished no consideration. The present theory concerns housing furnished in connection with employment, a recognized employee-tenant setting. Thus, the material question is whether services or employment obligations constituted consideration for agreed occupancy—not simply whether Appellant wrote a rent check. [8]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The cited cases cease to be dispositive if Appellant’s services supplied consideration and the employment arrangement established occupancy terms; at minimum, their different consideration facts prevent a categorical extension at summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The phrase “proceedings under this chapter may be had” identifies when the statutory remedy is available; it does not, standing alone, authorize self-help or resolve whether another provision makes judicial process necessary. Moreover, Ohio FED law is not facially confined to landlord-tenant defendants: the statute defines classes of defendants against whom FED may be brought, including persons who are not tenants. [72]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if Appellant was not a Chapter 5321 tenant, the word “may” does not supply the missing proposition that Appellees were affirmatively entitled to remove her summarily without judicial process.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief improperly equates “not a tenant under Chapter 5321” with “outside Chapter 1923.” The retrieved authority explains that the FED statute does not limit defendants to tenants and instead identifies a broader statutory class against whom the action may be brought. Thus, Ogle and Stone may address a statutory tenant’s wrongful-eviction claim, but non-tenancy alone does not show that Chapter 1923 is irrelevant to an occupier of land. [72]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The brief cannot obtain affirmance merely by disproving Chapter 5321 tenancy; it must separately answer Appellant’s argument that she fell within Chapter 1923’s occupier-of-land provision and explain why that provision permitted self-help.

attacks_proposed.argument: Northfield Park does not support the broad proposition asserted here. As quoted in the supplied material, that decision concerned a commercial lease containing a voluntarily accepted self-help provision and repossession occurring without breach of the peace and with the lessee’s acquiescence. This case concerns residential occupancy, and the brief identifies no comparable contractual self-help provision or acquiescence. The decision’s commercial-premises reasoning therefore cannot establish a general self-help right against residential occupants.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without extending a narrowly described commercial-lease holding beyond its facts, the brief lacks authority for its central claim that a residential homeowner may summarily remove every non-tenant occupant.

attacks_proposed.argument: The categorical assertion that employee housing receives statutory protection only when there is a “separate” rental agreement and cash rent adds requirements not contained in the cited definition. A rental agreement may be oral and may be the agreement establishing terms concerning occupancy; retrieved Ohio landlord-tenant authority specifically recognizes that an employee may lease and reside in residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment. [2, 6, 8]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the employment agreement itself can govern residential occupancy, the brief cannot exclude live-in caregivers, nannies, clergy, and every other listed employee category as a matter of law merely because there was no separate lease or cash-rent payment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The supplied record material does not substantiate the current-case factual premises that no oral occupancy agreement existed, that the room was only an accommodation, or that Appellant furnished no consideration for occupancy. It supports only the general proposition applied in Ogle, Stone, and Amick. Because the dispositive question is whether the parties’ employment and occupancy arrangement amounted to a rental agreement, the cited general rule cannot substitute for evidence resolving that question here.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Absent record support for the decisive current-case facts, Appellee has not established the factual predicate for affirming summary judgment on the no-tenancy theory.

attacks_proposed.argument: Reynolds may involve a different claim and procedural posture, but the distinction does not answer the substantive point for which its facts matter: the brief itself describes a live-in nurse claiming occupancy rights as payment for nursing and housekeeping services. That circumstance undercuts the brief’s categorical assumption that employee services cannot serve as consideration for residential occupancy merely because no cash rent is paid. Ohio employee-tenant authority likewise recognizes residential occupancy pursuant to an employment contract. [8]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if Reynolds is not controlling on jurisdiction or remedy, its employment-for-occupancy facts reinforce that the nature of the parties’ bargain must be examined and cannot be disposed of solely by asking whether cash rent changed hands.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Estate’s separate no-involvement theory is not established by the supplied record material. The asserted deposition facts concerning who jointly decided to terminate Appellant, who directed her departure, and John Wallace’s role are not supported in the supplied record. Physical absence when the removal occurred would not, without evidence addressing prior authorization or participation, establish complete noninvolvement.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The Estate cannot obtain an independent affirmance on a no-participation ground when the evidentiary premise for that ground is absent from the supplied record.

attacks_proposed.argument: The requested affirmance depends on treating disputed legal inferences as established facts: that employment-linked occupancy cannot constitute a rental agreement, that services cannot constitute consideration, and that the permissive wording of R.C. 1923.02 affirmatively authorizes residential self-help. The statutory definitions and employee-tenant authority do not establish those propositions, while Chapter 1923 expressly encompasses defendants beyond conventional tenants. [2, 6, 8, 72]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Because the brief’s dispositive premises are neither legally compelled nor adequately supported by the supplied record, its conclusion that all appealed wrongful-eviction counts fail as a matter of law does not follow.

judge_assessments.assessment: This reaches the brief’s central vulnerability. R.C. 5321.01 turns on entitlement under a written or oral rental agreement, not on a document labeled a lease or payment of cash rent. The employee-tenant material confirms that an employment contract can sometimes supply the occupancy arrangement. It does not establish that Lee was such a tenant, however. The cited record portrays the room as available only while she was on duty, ties possession to at-will employment, and shows that she maintained another residence. The decisive question is whether the evidence, construed for Lee, permits an inference that services were consideration for an enforceable right to exclusive residential occupancy rather than merely permission to sleep there while working. If it does, the categorical no-rent/no-tenancy reasoning cannot sustain summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says there was no oral or written rental agreement, Lee paid no rent, the room was an employment accommodation, she stayed overnight only because Wallace needed care, and she maintained a separate residence. It relies on Ogle, Stone, and Amick for the rule that an occupant without a rental agreement and rent is not a tenant.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete 2007 versions of R.C. 5321.01, the full employee-tenant authorities summarized in source 8, and the deposition testimony concerning the agreed compensation and Lee’s control over the room would settle the issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack correctly identifies a statutory-logic gap. The words “may be had” identify circumstances in which an FED proceeding is available; they do not themselves create a substantive privilege to use self-help. Source 72 also confirms that Chapter 1923 reaches defined defendants beyond conventional tenants. But that source does not establish that FED is exclusive for every occupier, so it does not itself prove Lee’s ultimate position. The brief has a substantial response in R.C. 5321.15(A), Ogle, and Stone, which it reads as making exclusivity depend on residential tenancy. Still, the brief’s reliance on the isolated word “may” contributes little. If the cited wrongful-eviction cases do not govern this employment-linked occupancy, the brief lacks a clear affirmative source authorizing summary removal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes “Proceedings under this chapter may be had as follows,” argues that the legislature made FED exclusive only for residential landlord-tenant relationships through R.C. 5321.15(A), and relies on Ogle, Stone, Northfield Park, and commercial self-help cases.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research should focus on Ohio appellate decisions addressing whether Chapter 1923 or common-law ejectment rules prohibit self-help against a residential licensee or employee occupant who is not a Chapter 5321 tenant.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief’s categorical statement that protection exists only when an employee has a separate rental agreement and pays cash rent is broader than the cited statutory definition. R.C. 5321.01 does not expressly require that the occupancy agreement be separate from an employment contract, and the employee-tenant material indicates that employment and tenancy can coexist. Thus the brief cannot defend its sweeping list of caregivers, nannies, clergy, and other workers on statutory text alone. The defect does not automatically make Lee a tenant: the record may still establish that her room was a revocable workplace accommodation rather than premises she was entitled to occupy to the exclusion of others. The advocate risks losing the categorical legal rule and having the case judged under the actual terms of Lee’s arrangement.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that employee occupants receive FED protection only if they entered a separate rental agreement or lease and paid rent pursuant to that agreement. It characterizes Lee’s room as an accommodation incident to at-will employment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full employee-tenant discussion and controlling Ohio cases should be examined to determine what possession, exclusivity, and consideration are required when lodging forms part of compensation.

judge_assessments.assessment: The distinctions are legitimate. As the brief describes them, Ogle and Stone involved gratuitous domestic occupancy, and Amick expressly found both no agreement and no consideration. Lee, by contrast, was required to remain overnight to perform paid services. Those differences prevent treating the cases as mechanically dispositive without examining the employment bargain. The attack overreaches to the extent it assumes that services were consideration for the room: services may have been exchanged solely for wages, with overnight access remaining a revocable license. The brief has evidence supporting that characterization, but it does not squarely analyze whether the employment agreement allocated part of Lee’s compensation to an exclusive possessory right.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief describes Ogle, Stone, and Amick at length, emphasizes the absence of rent and any rental agreement, and says Lee’s room was supplied only as an employment accommodation. It does not separately analyze whether her services constituted consideration for occupancy.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The compensation terms, Lee’s right to use the room when off duty, the family’s access to it, and any testimony describing lodging as part of compensation would determine how persuasive the distinctions are.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack lands, although its assertion that the relevant facts are absent is inaccurate. The brief itself states that John Wallace and Sally Wallace jointly decided to terminate Lee. That evidence conflicts with the later assertion that the Estate had “no involvement.” John’s physical absence during the removal and Lee’s testimony that he did not personally order her out do not negate prior authorization or participation in the joint decision. The brief supplies no legal authority making physical presence an element of liability. If the removal was otherwise wrongful, this record does not clearly provide the Estate an independent no-participation ground for affirmance.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says John and Sally Wallace jointly made the termination decision, but also says John was absent when Lee was removed, did not personally terminate her or order her departure, treated her fairly, and therefore had no involvement in the removal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The pleaded theory against John, agency evidence concerning Sally’s power of attorney, and Ohio authority on authorization or concerted participation in wrongful eviction would determine the Estate’s exposure.

judge_assessments.assessment: Northfield Park cannot carry the residential self-help proposition asserted here. As the brief’s own quotation shows, that case involved a commercial lease containing an agreed self-help provision, peaceful repossession, and the lessee’s acquiescence. Those limitations are absent here. The decision is useful only by analogy for the narrower proposition that Chapter 1923 is not universally exclusive. The brief does not lose its entire position because Ogle and Stone address residential lockouts more directly, but it loses Northfield Park as affirmative authority for a general right to remove non-tenant residential occupants summarily.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges that Northfield Park involved a commercial lease and quotes its reliance on an express self-help clause, lack of breach of peace, and acquiescence. It uses the case to argue that the legislature prohibited residential landlord self-help through R.C. 5321.15(A) but did not make Chapter 1923 exclusive in every other setting.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio cases applying Northfield Park outside commercial leases, especially to residential licensees or employee occupants, would determine whether the analogy has any broader force.

judge_assessments.assessment: This misstates the brief. The brief does not say Chapter 1923 is irrelevant to non-tenants; it acknowledges that an owner may elect FED against an occupier and discusses Amick as an example. Its position is that FED is not the exclusive remedy absent a residential tenancy. Source 72 establishes that FED may be brought against persons other than tenants, but it does not establish exclusivity or prohibit self-help. The attack therefore duplicates the valid portion of a3 without answering the brief’s actual distinction between availability and exclusivity.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly recognizes FED as an available remedy for a non-tenant but argues that it is optional rather than exclusive.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Authority addressing exclusivity of FED against non-tenant residential occupiers, rather than merely their eligibility as FED defendants, would be necessary.

judge_assessments.assessment: Reynolds does not materially undermine the brief on this record. It shows that services can be alleged as consideration for a leasehold, but the brief describes an express promise of a lifetime leasehold and a quiet-title or jurisdictional dispute. Lee’s record, as presented, contains no comparable promise. Reynolds therefore supports only the abstract proposition already captured by the employee-tenant authorities; it does not make Lee’s employment arrangement a rental agreement or control the wrongful-eviction issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief distinguishes Reynolds because it involved an alleged lifetime leasehold promised as compensation and appellate issues concerning quiet title and subject-matter jurisdiction.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full Reynolds opinions would confirm whether they announced any rule about employee tenancy beyond the pleaded lifetime-interest claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The claim of complete evidentiary absence misreads the supplied brief. The brief cites deposition testimony that Lee was required to stay overnight while on duty, was given a room as an employment accommodation, paid no rent, had no deduction for rent, understood her employment was at will, and maintained another residence. Those facts support the license or accommodation characterization. Whether they conclusively negate an oral occupancy agreement is a legitimate summary-judgment question, but that is the legal-inference problem raised by a1, not an absence of record support.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief provides deposition citations for the room’s employment purpose, the lack of rent, Lee’s at-will status, and her separate residence, and characterizes the facts as undisputed.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual deposition excerpts and summary-judgment exhibits would show whether Lee offered contrary evidence of an agreed possessory right.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is an omnibus restatement of a1, a3, and a6 rather than an independent procedural defect. Summary judgment may rest on undisputed historical facts and legal characterization; calling the disputed propositions “legal inferences” does not itself defeat affirmance. The specific tenancy and self-help issues are substantial, but they should be evaluated directly rather than repackaged as a defect in the requested relief.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The conclusion incorporates the preceding arguments that Lee was not a tenant, FED was not exclusive, and the appealed counts consequently failed as a matter of law.

judge_assessments.assessment: The court would not reach this attack. Appellees did not institute an FED action against Lee and do not claim that they served an R.C. 1923.04 notice. The brief’s statement that proper R.C. 1923.04 notice was given concerns the separate Amick litigation. The Estate did not assume a current-case notice element merely by citing that case or the statute.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief discusses compliance with R.C. 1923.04 only while describing why the FED judgment in Amick survived a notice challenge.

judge_assessments.assessment: This duplicates r11 and rests on the same category error. Because no FED proceeding was filed in this case, the statutory wording required in an R.C. 1923.04 notice is not an element the Estate undertook to prove. The real dispute is whether judicial process was required at all.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief does not assert that Lee received an R.C. 1923.04 notice; it argues that no FED action or associated notice was required.

judge_assessments.assessment: The actual ground stated in an R.C. 1923.04 notice is immaterial because the current removal did not proceed through FED and the brief does not rely on any such notice. The employment termination is identified as the reason Lee was asked to leave, but the adequacy of a statutory notice was never made an element of Appellees’ position. The attack would be discarded without reaching the merits.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lee was terminated from at-will employment and immediately asked to leave; its R.C. 1923.04 discussion concerns Amick rather than Lee.

results.verdict: Partly persuasive but exposed on the central tenancy questio
results.assessment: The brief has a workable core: it correctly resists treating the absence of a labeled lease or cash rent as automatically dispositive, and it distinguishes the self-help language in Chapter 1923 from a standalone authorization. But it is vulnerable because it overstates the “separate rental agreement and rent” point, leans too heavily on Northfield Park outside its commercial, consensual setting, and does not fully answer whether the employment arrangement itself gave Appellant an enforceable right to occupy the room. The no-involvement theory is also thin if the record reflects a joint termination decision or prior authorization. The research leaves the key factual issue unresolved: whether services were consideration for exclusive occupancy or only for wages.

Employee housing can, in an appropriate case, be governed by a rental agreement arising from employment. Still, the retrieved authority also states that a rent obligation is a prerequisite, and this record is described as showing no rent, no deduction from wages, a room available only while on duty, and a separately maintained residence. The attack exposes an analysis the brief could have developed better, but it does not identify evidence that Lee's services were consideration for a possessory right independent of her work duties.
challenges.suggested_response: Ohio law recognizes that an employee may occupy residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment, but the supplied record does not show that this arrangement created a tenancy. The record shows that appellant was provided a room to stay in while on duty as an accommodation for her employment, that she paid no rent, that nothing was deducted from her paycheck for rent, and that she maintained a separate residence. Under the authorities appellant cites, an obligation to pay rent is a prerequisite to a landlord-tenant relationship, and that prerequisite is absent here.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the focus on the absence of rent, rental agreement, and consideration; do not let the brief drift into an undeveloped employee-tenant theory. If appellant argues employment housing created a tenancy, answer that this record does not show the kind of agreement or rent obligation Ohio law treats as necessary.

attacks_proposed.argument: The argument does not reconcile its tenant-focused reading of R.C. 5321.15(A) with Chapter 1923's broader reach. Authority describing Ohio FED procedure states that the statute does not facially restrict defendants to tenants and that R.C. 1923.02 defines the classes against whom an FED action may be brought. The inclusion of an occupier without color of title therefore cannot be dismissed merely because R.C. 5321.15(A) separately protects residential tenants.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Chapter 1923 expressly supplies a possession procedure against non-tenant occupiers, the limitation in R.C. 5321.15(A) does not itself establish a right to bypass judicial process.

Ohio landlord-tenant authority recognizes that an employee may lease and reside in residential premises pursuant to an employment contract. attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The employment relationship cannot be treated as legally incapable of creating a tenancy. Appellees had to establish the terms and consideration of this particular employment-housing arrangement rather than rely on labels alone.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attacks a central link in the motion. Ohio law distinguishes delivery from recording, and the cited source supports the general proposition that lack of recording does not prevent passage of title; it does not establish that delivery to the probate court was ineffective or that no delivery occurred. The brief expressly asserts that the deed was delivered to the probate court and cites Gordon for treating that event as delivery, so the attack overstates matters when it says the motion shows only execution. But counsel's assertion is not itself Civ.R. 56 evidence. If Exhibits 10 and 13 do not establish the fact and circumstances of delivery, including the grantors' intent to relinquish control, plaintiff has not conclusively proved present title. Because present title anchors the possession theory, that evidentiary omission would defeat summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: The probate court ordered the Cedar Road property transferred into the Estate, and defendants thereafter executed a deed conveying the property to the Estate. Ohio law does not require recording to pass title; the Estate therefore relies on the probate order and the executed deed as the Civ.R. 56 evidence of its present title and right to possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rest the title argument on an unsupported assertion that delivery to the probate court itself passed title. Keep the probate order and executed deed, but if the record does not contain a Civ.R. 56 material proving delivery and relinquishment of control, the brief should concede that gap rather than overstate the point.

That is particularly insufficient because plaintiff's own factual account acknowledges a prior transfer of the Cedar Road property to defendants, while the effectiveness of the asserted reconveyance depends on the unresolved delivery issue.

challenges.judge_assessment: R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) supports the stated statutory requirements, but it does not by itself establish that defendants' former deed remains color of title after the probate adjudication and their subsequent conveyance. The brief does more than point to defendants' lack of proof: it relies on the probate court's determination that their title was invalid, orders directing return of the property, and the deed they later executed. Those materials answer the attack if properly authenticated and legally effective. The attack becomes consequential only if plaintiff cannot prove delivery of the reconveyance or the operative effect of the probate orders. Otherwise, the prior transfer does not create a genuine issue merely because defendants once possessed a deed.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) is satisfied here because the probate court ordered the Cedar Road property returned to the Estate, and defendants thereafter executed the deed conveying the property to the Estate. On this record, defendants occupy the Premises without a superior title interest, and the Estate, as the party entitled to present possession, may maintain this forcible entry and detainer action.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Frame the possession element directly under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5): the Estate’s present title and the defendants’ continued occupancy without lawful title support the right to possession. Do not argue merely that defendants failed to prove color of title; state the affirmative basis for the Estate’s possessory right.

challenges.judge_assessment: The procedural proposition is correct but adds nothing independent. Plaintiff must satisfy its initial Civ.R. 56 burden, and the phrase 'presented and to be presented' cannot substitute for admissible evidence. The motion, however, does identify and incorporate affidavits and exhibits concerning the probate orders, deed, occupancy, and notice. Whether those materials are sufficient depends on the specific delivery and possession issues addressed elsewhere; it cannot be decided merely from the motion's introductory wording. As framed, this is a generalized restatement of the summary-judgment standard rather than a separate ground for denial.
challenges.suggested_response: The Estate has supported this motion with sworn affidavits and exhibits showing the probate court’s transfer orders, the executed deed conveying the Cedar Road property to the Estate, defendants’ continued possession of the Premises, and service of the statutory notice. Those Civ.R. 56 materials establish the absence of a genuine issue of material fact as to the Estate’s entitlement to present possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the summary-judgment standard, but tie it to the actual Civ.R. 56 materials rather than to conclusory language about evidence ‘presented and to be presented.’ The motion should say what in the record establishes each element, not merely recite the standard.

attacks_proposed.argument: Plaintiff has not established the delivery necessary for the deed to pass title. Plaintiff's own rule requires both proper execution and delivery, while the supplied materials show only that the deed was executed and remained unrecorded. The further assertion that delivery to the probate court constituted delivery of title is not independently supported by the supplied record. The fact that recording is unnecessary does not eliminate the separately stated delivery requirement.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without competent evidence of delivery, plaintiff has not established present title as a matter of law, and its possession claim cannot be resolved on summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) requires plaintiff to establish both that defendants occupy without color of title and that plaintiff has the right of possession. The motion instead says defendants are living there 'without proof of color of title,' improperly treating defendants' lack of proof as affirmative proof of plaintiff's statutory element. That is particularly insufficient because plaintiff's own factual account acknowledges a prior transfer of the Cedar Road property to defendants, while the effectiveness of the asserted reconveyance depends on the unresolved delivery issue.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Unless plaintiff affirmatively eliminates a genuine dispute over the absence of color of title, it cannot obtain judgment under the statutory theory it invoked.

attacks_proposed.argument: The probate order authorizing the Executor to manage the properties does not, standing alone, establish the statutory right to immediate possession against these defendants. The quoted order concerns management functions, while R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) separately requires a present right of possession. Plaintiff's notice asserting that the Estate has title and possession is plaintiff's own assertion, not an independent adjudication or evidentiary substitute for that element. Sed is distinguishable on the motion's own description because the property there had been found to belong to the probate estate; here, plaintiff's proof of consummated title transfer remains incomplete.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Management authority cannot fill the evidentiary gap concerning present title and the immediate right to exclude defendants. Without that link, the superior-possession conclusion is not established as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The general availability of summary judgment in a forcible-entry-and-detainer action does not establish entitlement to it here. Under the standard recited in the motion, plaintiff must first identify Civ.R. 56 materials eliminating genuine disputes on every essential element. Statements that the evidence 'presented and to be presented' shows no dispute are conclusions, and the supplied record only partially supports the dispositive propositions concerning deed delivery and the superior present right to possession.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Because plaintiff has not discharged its initial burden on title and present possession, the burden does not shift to defendants and summary judgment must be denied regardless of whether defendants rely on their pleadings.

attacks_proposed.argument: The analogy to Usha Pillai assumes the very point plaintiff must prove. As the motion describes that case, there was no question about present title because a prior proceeding had determined it. Here, the supplied materials show an order directing transfer and an executed but unrecorded deed, but do not independently establish the asserted delivery to the probate court. Ohio authority recognizes that present ownership may control possession, but that principle does not decide a disputed or inadequately supported premise of present ownership.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If present title has not been conclusively established, the court cannot use the present-title doctrine to bypass the missing proof or declare that no title issue remains.

attacks_proposed.argument: A writ of execution follows only when a judgment of restitution has been entered and the plaintiff requests the writ. It is therefore not an independent consequence of showing occupancy and notice. Because plaintiff has not conclusively established deed delivery, absence of color of title, and a superior present right to possession, the predicate judgment of restitution cannot yet be entered.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The requested writ must be denied unless and until plaintiff proves entitlement to a judgment of restitution on all statutory elements.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attacks a central link in the motion. Ohio law distinguishes delivery from recording, and the cited source supports the general proposition that lack of recording does not prevent passage of title; it does not establish that delivery to the probate court was ineffective or that no delivery occurred. The brief expressly asserts that the deed was delivered to the probate court and cites Gordon for treating that event as delivery, so the attack overstates matters when it says the motion shows only execution. But counsel's assertion is not itself Civ.R. 56 evidence. If Exhibits 10 and 13 do not establish the fact and circumstances of delivery, including the grantors' intent to relinquish control, plaintiff has not conclusively proved present title. Because present title anchors the possession theory, that evidentiary omission would defeat summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says defendants executed the deed on February 1, 2023, cites Exhibits 10 and 13, expressly states that the deed was delivered to the probate court, and cites Gordon v. Bartlett for the proposition that this constituted delivery of title.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review Exhibits 10 and 13 and the full text of Gordon v. Bartlett to determine whether admissible evidence shows delivery and whether delivery to the court under these circumstances legally completed the conveyance.

judge_assessments.assessment: R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) supports the stated statutory requirements, but it does not by itself establish that defendants' former deed remains color of title after the probate adjudication and their subsequent conveyance. The brief does more than point to defendants' lack of proof: it relies on the probate court's determination that their title was invalid, orders directing return of the property, and the deed they later executed. Those materials answer the attack if properly authenticated and legally effective. The attack becomes consequential only if plaintiff cannot prove delivery of the reconveyance or the operative effect of the probate orders. Otherwise, the prior transfer does not create a genuine issue merely because defendants once possessed a deed.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges the 2021 transfer to defendants but says the probate court determined that defendants lacked valid title, ordered them to convey the property to the Estate, and that defendants executed the resulting deed in February 2023.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full probate orders, both deeds, and Ohio authority defining continuing 'color of title' after an adverse title adjudication and reconveyance would settle the issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: The procedural proposition is correct but adds nothing independent. Plaintiff must satisfy its initial Civ.R. 56 burden, and the phrase 'presented and to be presented' cannot substitute for admissible evidence. The motion, however, does identify and incorporate affidavits and exhibits concerning the probate orders, deed, occupancy, and notice. Whether those materials are sufficient depends on the specific delivery and possession issues addressed elsewhere; it cannot be decided merely from the motion's introductory wording. As framed, this is a generalized restatement of the summary-judgment standard rather than a separate ground for denial.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief correctly recites the Civ.R. 56 and Dresher standards and incorporates affidavits from the property manager and counsel, together with their attached exhibits.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the incorporated affidavits and exhibits for personal knowledge, authentication, and proof of deed delivery and present possession.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source supports the general present-title doctrine, not the assertion that title remains unresolved here. The brief does not rely solely on an executed, unrecorded deed; it also relies on a prior probate determination, repeated orders requiring return, and asserted delivery of the deed to the probate court. That is materially similar to the prior adjudication described in Usha Pillai. Any genuine weakness is the evidentiary and legal sufficiency of delivery, already captured by a1. This framing attack would not independently affect the result.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief analogizes the case to Usha Pillai because the probate court had already determined defendants lacked valid title and ordered conveyance, after which defendants executed and allegedly delivered the deed.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full Usha Pillai opinion and the probate orders would confirm whether the prior adjudication is sufficiently final and comparable, but the deed-delivery issue remains the dispositive factual question.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack is not supported by the cited sources as a distinct legal objection. R.C. 1923.02 requires a right to possession, but the cited general jurisdiction statute does not establish that court-authorized management and sale powers are legally insufficient. More importantly, the brief does not rely on management authority standing alone. It also relies on the probate title determination, return orders, and deed. Sed, as the brief describes it, affirmatively supports the proposition that authority to sell estate property can provide a superior possessory right. The proposed distinction merely repeats the unresolved-delivery issue and does not undermine the independent probate orders.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief combines the Estate's asserted title with probate orders authorizing administration, management, and sale, and cites Sed for the conclusion that authority to sell estate real property supplies a superior right to possession.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full text of Sed and the precise probate orders would determine the scope of the Estate's authority, but the supplied sources do not support this attack as framed.

judge_assessments.assessment: This misreads the brief. The motion expressly says the notice was served at the Premises and cites Exhibits 3 and 12. R.C. 1923.04(A) permits service by leaving the notice at the premises, and the retrieved authority confirms that physical delivery to a person is unnecessary under that method. There could be an evidentiary problem if the exhibits merely use the conclusory word 'served' without showing that the notice was actually left there, but the categorical assertion that the brief does not identify any permitted method is incorrect.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says defendants were served on June 28, 2023, that the notice was served at the Premises, that the action was filed on August 9, 2023, and that the notice contained the required language in bold print.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review Exhibits 3 and 12 to confirm that an affiant with personal knowledge states that the notice was actually left at the Premises.

judge_assessments.assessment: R.C. 1923.13 confirms that a writ follows a judgment of restitution upon request, but the brief does not contend that occupancy and notice alone create an independent right to a writ. It asks the court first to enter judgment on the possession claim and then issue the writ. The attack therefore states the statutory sequence without identifying a separate defect. If title, possession, or notice remains genuinely disputed, judgment and the writ must both be withheld, but that consequence rises or falls with the underlying attacks rather than this remedy argument.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The conclusion asks for judgment as a matter of law on the possession claim and states that a writ of restitution should then issue.

results.verdict: partly persuasive but vulnerable on the central title-and-po
results.assessment: The motion has a plausible structure because it ties the possession claim to the probate orders, the executed deed, occupancy, and notice, but its weakest point is still the one that matters most: it does not cleanly prove delivery or otherwise conclusively establish present title, and counsel’s assertion cannot do that by itself. The color-of-title argument is also shaky to the extent it leans on defendants’ lack of proof rather than affirmative proof of the Estate’s right to possession. The procedural objection is the least powerful because it mostly restates the summary-judgment standard. The research did not settle whether the probate-order/deed combination is enough without clearer Civ.R. 56 evidence of delivery and effect.

record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: "On June 28, 2023 I served a Three-Day-Notice for the occupants to Leave the Premises at 8127 Cedar Road, Chesterland, Ohio 44026." ... "The purpose of this letter is to ask you to LEAVE the premises..." ... "Your compliance with this notice within 3 days after its service will prevent any further eviction action against you. YOU ARE BEING ASKED TO LEAVE THE PREMISES. IF YOU DO NOT LEAVE, AN EVICTION ACTION MAY BE INITIATED AGAINST YOU."

challenges.judge_assessment: This would land as a potentially dispositive evidentiary objection. R.C. 1923.04(A), supported by sources 48 and 50, limits service to specified methods, and source 49 treats the notice prerequisite as essential to commencing the action. The memorandum asserts certified mail, return receipt requested, but an assertion in the memorandum is not Civ.R. 56 evidence. If Exhibits 3 and 12 establish only that notice was served “at” the property and do not show certified mailing, personal delivery, or leaving the notice there, the Estate has not conclusively established compliance. The immediate consequence is denial of summary judgment; dismissal would follow only if the record affirmatively establishes defective notice rather than merely inadequate summary-judgment proof.
challenges.suggested_response: On June 28, 2023, plaintiff served the Three-Day Notice at the Premises located at 8127 Cedar Road, Chesterland, Ohio 44026, and the notice contained the statutory warning language required by R.C. 1923.04(A). The notice was served more than three days before this action was filed.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on the memorandum's bare reference to certified mail unless the exhibit actually shows that fact. Revise the notice paragraph to use only the service method the record affirmatively shows, or else supply the missing exhibit language before filing.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Estate treats defendants' supposed failure to produce proof of color of title as affirmative proof that they have none. But the Estate selected R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), which applies to an occupier “without color of title,” and therefore the Estate must affirmatively establish that condition before the summary-judgment burden shifts. The supplied excerpts contain that proposition only in the Estate's own notice and motion-to-show-cause characterization; they do not identify independent evidence addressing every claimed basis on which defendants occupy the property. Ohio authority also recognizes that an occupant may assert an ownership interest independent of the purported landowner to defeat eviction.
challenges.why_it_matters: Present title alone does not complete the particular statutory theory pleaded under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5). A failure of proof on the separate no-color-of-title element precludes judgment as a matter of law.

record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: "you occupy the premises without color of title, and the Estate of Anthony Notarian has title and the right to possession; you have no rental agreement and are not a tenant; you have not paid any rent; you were ordered to return title and possession of the real property to the Estate of Anthony Notarian by the Court of Common Pleas..." and "the Defendants ... failed to return real property belonging to the Estate of Anthony Notarian, and are in violation of Orders issued by this Court."

challenges.judge_assessment: The statutory point is sound: under the Estate's chosen R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) theory, occupation without color of title is part of the basis for relief, and the Estate cannot shift its initial Civ.R. 56 burden merely by saying defendants produced no proof. Source 22 also recognizes that an occupant may defeat eviction by asserting an ownership interest independent of the plaintiff's claimed title. On this record, however, the Estate has a substantial answer: it relies on a probate adjudication rejecting defendants' title and a later deed by which defendants conveyed the property to the Estate. Those materials may affirmatively negate any current color of title derived from defendants' former deed. The attack becomes serious only if defendants identify another existing written instrument or independent ownership claim, or if the probate order and deed are not competent Civ.R. 56 evidence.
challenges.suggested_response: The Probate Court ordered the Cedar Road Premises transferred to the Estate, and defendants thereafter executed a deed conveying the Premises to the Estate on February 1, 2023. Under those orders and the executed deed, defendants are occupants without color of title, and the Estate has present title and the superior right to possession. See Usha Pillai IRA LLC v. Roseman, 8th Dist. Cuyahoga No. 112524, 2023-Ohio-3480, paragraph 18; Haas v. Gerski, 175 Ohio St. 327, 330 (1963).
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Recast the title/color-of-title point as an affirmative record showing, not as a complaint that defendants failed to disprove it. The paragraph should say the probate order and deed eliminated any current title claim in defendants and left the Estate with present title and the right to possession.

challenges.judge_assessment: The general Civ.R. 56 concern is legitimate, but this attack is too abstract and is not supported by its cited source. Source 1 merely reflects a trial court's use of Civ.R. 56 and does not establish the movant's record-production burden. More importantly, the brief does more than merely identify unspecified affidavits: it incorporates the property manager's and counsel's affidavits and identifies exhibits for title, possession, and notice. The phrase “presented and to be presented” cannot support judgment, but the court would decide the motion from the materials actually filed rather than deny it because of that phrase. Any concrete foundation defect should be raised against a particular affidavit or exhibit, as attack a2 does.
challenges.suggested_response: Plaintiff supports this Motion with the affidavit of the property manager and the affidavit of undersigned counsel, together with the attached probate orders, deed, and notice exhibits incorporated by reference. Those materials show that the Estate has title and the right to present possession, and that plaintiff gave the notice required before filing this action.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the Civ.R. 56 paragraph to point to the actual affidavits and attached exhibits rather than speaking abstractly about evidence. The brief does not need a new authority; it needs a cleaner record citation tying the affidavits to title, possession, and notice.

attacks_proposed.argument: The motion does not satisfy its initial summary-judgment burden merely by identifying affidavits and exhibits. The supplied record establishes only that the property manager and counsel made affidavits “in support” of the motion; it does not establish that their contents, attachments, and personal-knowledge foundations eliminate every genuine dispute concerning notice, lack of color of title, and present possession. The promise to rely on evidence “presented and to be presented” likewise cannot establish the absence of a genuine issue on the materials presently before the Court.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Unless the Estate first makes a complete, competent, record-specific showing on every element of its possession claim, the burden never shifts to defendants and partial summary judgment must be denied.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Estate has not conclusively proved a statutorily authorized method of serving the three-day notice. R.C. 1923.04(A) permits certified mail with return receipt requested, personal delivery, or leaving the notice at the usual abode or premises. The supplied affidavit says only that the affiant “served” the notice “at” the property. It does not establish certified mailing and a return-receipt request, personal delivery, or the act of leaving the notice at the premises. That conclusory description is not the same as proof of one of the statute's specified methods.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Proper notice is a prerequisite to commencing the forcible-entry-and-detainer action. Failure to prove a permitted service method defeats summary judgment and may require dismissal of the possession claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The supplied record does not establish when this action was commenced. It shows notice dated June 28, 2023, but it does not supply a docket-stamped complaint or other Civ.R. 56 material proving the asserted August 9, 2023 filing date. Because R.C. 1923.04(A) requires notice three or more days before beginning the action, evidence of the notice date alone does not establish compliance.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without competent proof of both service and commencement dates, the Estate cannot establish the statutory waiting period as an undisputed fact.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Estate treats defendants' supposed failure to produce proof of color of title as affirmative proof that they have none. But the Estate selected R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), which applies to an occupier “without color of title,” and therefore the Estate must affirmatively establish that condition before the summary-judgment burden shifts. The supplied excerpts contain that proposition only in the Estate's own notice and motion-to-show-cause characterization; they do not identify independent evidence addressing every claimed basis on which defendants occupy the property. Ohio authority also recognizes that an occupant may assert an ownership interest independent of the purported landowner to defeat eviction.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Present title alone does not complete the particular statutory theory pleaded under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5). A failure of proof on the separate no-color-of-title element precludes judgment as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that defendants are occupying the property “in violation of court orders” is not conclusively established by the supplied orders. The quoted probate order directs transfer of the real property into the Estate, and the later order authorizes the Estate to manage it. The supplied statement that defendants were ordered to return possession appears in the Estate's notice and motion to show cause, not in the quoted operative language of the orders themselves. The deed evidence may establish transfer of title, but it does not by itself prove violation of an express vacatur command.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The Court cannot use an unproven contempt or order-violation theory as a substitute for determining each statutory element of the independent forcible-entry-and-detainer claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The title evidence does not entitle the Estate to summary judgment by itself. Ohio materials state that present possession may depend on present record title, while also recognizing that an occupant can assert an independent ownership interest to defeat eviction. Thus, even if the probate order and quitclaim deed establish the Estate's title, the Court still must separately decide whether the Estate has proved the statutory basis for dispossessing these particular occupants, including the absence of color of title and compliance with pre-suit notice.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This prevents the Estate from collapsing proof of title into automatic proof of every element required for restitution under R.C. Chapter 1923.

attacks_proposed.argument: A writ is not an automatic consequence of showing record title. R.C. 1923.13 authorizes a writ of execution when a judgment of restitution has been entered in an action under Chapter 1923. Because the Estate has not conclusively established the statutory notice method, commencement timing, and no-color-of-title element on the supplied record, the predicate judgment of restitution has not yet been justified.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if the Court accepts the Estate's title evidence, it should deny the requested writ unless and until the Estate proves entitlement to a judgment of restitution under Chapter 1923.

Source 1 merely reflects a trial court's use of Civ.R. 56 and does not establish the movant's record-production burden. More importantly, the brief does more than merely identify unspecified affidavits: it incorporates the property manager's and counsel's affidavits and identifies exhibits for title, possession, and notice. The phrase “presented and to be presented” cannot support judgment, but the court would decide the motion from the materials actually filed rather than deny it because of that phrase. judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete filed affidavits and exhibits would determine whether there are specific personal-knowledge, authentication, hearsay, or completeness defects.

judge_assessments.assessment: R.C. 1923.04(A) requires the notice to precede commencement by at least three days, but this court need not demand a separate docket-stamped copy of the complaint to establish when this very action was filed. The filing date is part of the court's own docket and can be verified directly. With an asserted June 28 notice and an August 9 filing, the timing margin is also far greater than three days. This attack matters only if the actual docket contradicts August 9 or the notice was not served on June 28.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that notice was served June 28, 2023, and that the action was filed August 9, 2023, citing Exhibits 12 and 3.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Confirm the complaint's file stamp and the actual service date. No broader research is needed.

judge_assessments.assessment: The quoted orders may not contain an express command that defendants personally vacate, so the brief should not characterize occupancy as contempt without the operative language. But violation of a probate order is not a necessary element of the R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) possession claim. The court can decide present title, right to possession, color of title, and notice without deciding contempt or construing the probate orders as express vacatur commands. The court therefore would not let this collateral point control summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the Probate Court ordered the Premises returned to the Estate, later authorized the Estate to manage the property, and that defendants remained in possession in violation of those orders.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete probate orders would settle whether they expressly required surrender of physical possession, but that issue is unnecessary unless the Estate relies on contempt as an independent ground for relief.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal distinction is correct but does not expose a framing error in the brief. The Estate does not rely on title alone: it separately invokes R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), alleges defendants lack color of title, describes their continued possession, and argues compliance with R.C. 1923.04(A). The real questions are whether the evidence proves those additional matters, addressed more precisely by attacks a2 and a4. Recasting the same issues as a title-versus-possession distinction adds little and risks suggesting the brief omitted arguments it actually made.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: In addition to present title, the brief argues that defendants occupy without color of title, that the Estate has a superior present right to possession, and that statutory notice was properly served before filing.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: No further research is needed beyond the evidence review identified for attacks a2 and a4.

judge_assessments.assessment: R.C. 1923.13 supports the proposition that a writ follows a judgment of restitution, but the brief asks the court to enter that predicate judgment through partial summary judgment and then issue the writ. It does not materially argue that record title alone authorizes a writ without judgment. Whether judgment is justified turns on the underlying statutory elements, not on a separate remedy-scope defect. This attack is therefore derivative of a2 and a4 rather than an independent ground for denial.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asks for partial summary judgment on the possession claim and concludes that, because the Estate has proved entitlement to present possession and complied with the required procedure, a writ of restitution should issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This duplicates attack a2 but supplies no legal authority and is less precise. The brief does not merely say that service happened; it expressly identifies certified mail, return receipt requested, and cites Exhibits 12 and 3. The viable objection is that those exhibits may fail to prove the asserted method, not that the brief omitted the method altogether. Keeping both attacks would overstate one evidentiary issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says service occurred by certified mail, return receipt requested, and cites Exhibits 12 and 3 as support.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: See the document review identified for attack a2.

judge_assessments.assessment: This duplicates attack a3, supplies no supporting authority, and overlooks that the commencement date is available from the docket of the pending case. A separate exhibit proving the court's own filing date ordinarily is unnecessary. There is no meaningful timing dispute unless the docket or service evidence contradicts the dates stated in the brief.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the action was filed August 9, 2023, more than a month after the asserted June 28 service date.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Confirm the complaint's file stamp and actual notice-service date.

results.assessment: The brief has a solid core if the probate orders and deed are competent Civ.R. 56 evidence, because they support the Estate’s claim to present possession and a superior right. Its biggest weakness is the three-day notice: the record described in the challenges does not clearly prove one of the statute’s required service methods, and the memorandum’s service assertion cannot fill that gap. It also needs a cleaner affirmative showing that defendants are occupants without color of title rather than relying on their failure to prove otherwise. The factual-support objection is secondary; the record is more than a bare promise, but the court will still need specific evidence tied to each element.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a legitimate threshold challenge because Baker relies on the municipal court's monetary cause of action, rather than the possession claim alone, to trigger Civ.R. 13(A). Sources 39 and 58 support the distinction: a possession-only eviction does not invoke compulsory-counterclaim preclusion, and statutory posting plus ordinary mail may be insufficient for a separate damages claim. But the attack overstates what Baker had to place in her initial summary-judgment submission. Baker submitted a certified judgment reciting that the court took evidence and awarded damages, and judgments of courts of record are ordinarily presumed valid unless the opposing party produces evidence of defective service or lack of jurisdiction. Friese's nonappearance, by itself, does not create a genuine issue. Thus this can defeat preclusion if Friese supplies the docket, return, or other Civ.R. 56 evidence showing service adequate only for possession, but it likely will not defeat summary judgment merely by pointing out that Baker did not attach service documents. The advocate risks shifting the burden incorrectly and inviting the court to treat the jurisdictional objection as speculative or an impe
challenges.suggested_response: Baker submitted certified copies of the municipal-court complaint and judgment showing that Baker asserted a separate monetary claim arising from the tenancy and that the municipal court entered a final judgment after hearing evidence. Friese has pointed to no Civ.R. 56 evidence that service on that monetary claim was defective, limited to possession only, or otherwise insufficient to support the court’s jurisdiction; a speculative objection does not create a genuine issue of material fact. The certified judgment therefore remains competent summary-judgment evidence that Baker’s prior monetary claim was finally adjudicated.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on the absence of service papers as a standalone weakness unless Friese has actually pointed to Civ.R. 56 evidence of defective service or lack of jurisdiction. Keep the res judicata argument tied to the certified municipal-court complaint and judgment, and add a sentence that Friese has offered no evidence that the separate damages claim was not properly before that court.

challenges.opponent_argument: Baker's categorical assertion that Ohio law imposes no statutory duty to install a stairway handrail addresses only R.C. 5321.04(A)(2)'s habitability requirement and ignores R.C. 5321.04(A)(1). Subsection (A)(1) independently requires compliance with applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes materially affecting health and safety, and Ohio authority specifically recognizes that a city code may impose a duty to install a handrail on a basement stairway. [26] Thus, even if St. Germain and Taylor foreclose treating a missing handrail, standing alone, as an (A)(2) habitability violation, they do not establish the broader proposition that no statutory handrail duty can exist.

challenges.judge_assessment: The cited authority supports this attack. Baker's cases, as presented, address only whether absence of a handrail by itself renders premises unfit or uninhabitable under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2). Source 26 identifies a distinct R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) route based on an applicable code and specifically references authority involving a city-code duty to install a basement-stairway handrail. Baker's categorical heading and conclusion—no statutory duty to install handrails—are therefore broader than her authorities establish. The brief does not answer the (A)(1) possibility. On the present record, however, the attack preserves only a potentially applicable theory: no particular Geauga County, township, state residential, or other code provision is identified, and the complaint apparently alleges merely that the stairs 'needed a railing.' If no code-based claim was pleaded or supported in opposition, the court need not invent one. The advocate stands to lose the categorical statutory ground, and possibly summary judgment on duty, if a governing code is timely identified; without that showing, the objection may not alter the result.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese’s Complaint alleges only ordinary premises liability and says only that the staircase “needed a railing.” It does not identify any applicable building, housing, health, or safety code, and it does not plead a separate R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) theory. On the claim actually pleaded, the absence of a handrail standing alone does not establish that the premises were unfit or uninhabitable under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2).
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the statutory-duty argument so it does not say Ohio law imposes no handrail duty in all circumstances. Limit the point to the authorities you actually have: the complaint does not plead a specific R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) code-violation theory, and the cited cases show that a missing handrail is not, by itself, an (A)(2) habitability violation.

challenges.judge_assessment: The legal distinction is correct. Armstrong and source 2 concern the common-law duty to warn or protect against known or obvious conditions; they do not erase an independent statutory code-compliance duty. Source 26 supports the possibility of such a duty for basement stairs. The brief itself partly recognizes this distinction by presenting its statutory argument in a separate subsection, so it does not rely solely on open and obvious to defeat all possible duties. The actual defect is that its statutory subsection addresses only (A)(2), not that its open-and-obvious discussion misstates Armstrong. This attack therefore lands as a limitation on the scope of u9, not an independent basis to deny the motion unless Friese has a viable (A)(1) theory. Overstating it as defeating the whole premises claim risks ignoring Baker's separate statutory argument and the complaint's apparent failure to plead a code violation.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese’s admitted knowledge of the stairway and the missing handrail defeats any common-law claim that Baker had a duty to warn him about an obvious condition he had used repeatedly for years. That point does not depend on any statutory theory. And Friese has not identified any applicable building or safety code that would impose a separate handrail requirement on this record; accordingly, the open-and-obvious analysis addresses the only duty theory actually pleaded.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the open-and-obvious discussion, but confine it to the common-law duty-to-warn claim. challenges.opponent_argument: The open-and-obvious doctrine cannot dispose of a negligence-per-se claim based on R.C. 5321.04. Ohio authority states that the doctrine does not apply to claims under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) or (A)(3), because a statutory violation constituting negligence per se obviates that common-law defense. [4] [6] Baker therefore cannot use Friese's familiarity with the stairs or knowledge that no handrail existed to defeat any adequately supported statutory-code claim.

But the attack assumes an 'adequately supported statutory-code claim,' which this record does not yet show. Baker's motion says the complaint asserts invitee premises liability and does not allege a landlord-statutory violation; the supplied facts identify no applicable code. Moreover, source 6 describes the rule for R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claims generally but cites Supreme Court holdings specifically concerning (A)(1) and (A)(3); Baker's (A)(2) argument is that there is no violation in the first place. Accordingly, this attack can preserve a pleaded and evidenced (A)(1) claim, but it cannot create one. The advocate risks devoting substantial argument to a defense Baker does not actually invoke against a viable statutory claim.
